rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dirhams below an uqiyya (forty) were counted rather than weighed, so small amounts were called countable.
rows.anchor: قيل تعد عدا ولا توزن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas gives the sale price as twenty dirhams.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس كانت عشرين درهما

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi gives the sale price as twenty-two dirhams.
rows.anchor: وعن السدي اثنين وعشرين درهما

rows.speaker: قالوا
rows.claim: A report says eleven brothers divided the money, two dirhams each, except Judah, who took nothing.
rows.anchor: قالوا والإخوة كانوا أحد عشر فكل واحد منهم أخذ درهمين إلا يهوذا لم يأخذ شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Joseph’s brothers sold him because they had little desire for him.
rows.anchor: لأنهم كانوا فيه من الزاهدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the water-carriers who found Joseph cared little for him or feared his rightful owner would reclaim him, so they sold him cheaply.
rows.anchor: لأنهم التقطوه والملتقط للشيء متهاون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation makes the buyers the ones who were indifferent to Joseph.
rows.anchor: أن الذين اشتروه كانوا فيه من الزاهدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “they were indifferent to it” may refer either to Joseph or to the low price.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون عائدا إلى الثمن البخس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the purchaser, whether from Joseph’s brothers or the water-carriers, took him to Egypt and sold him there.
rows.anchor: أن الذي اشتراه إما من الإخوة أو من الواردين على الماء ذهب به إلى مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports identify the purchaser as Qutayfir or Itifir, Egypt’s chief over the treasuries under King al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, an Amalekite who believed in Joseph and died in his lifetime.
rows.anchor: الذي اشتراه قطفير أو إطفير وهو العزيز الذي كان يلي خزائن مصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Qabus ibn Musab succeeded al-Rayyan, rejected Joseph’s call to Islam, and that Joseph was bought at seventeen and stayed in the master’s home thirteen years.
rows.anchor: فملك بعده قابوس بن مصعب فدعاه يوسف إلى الإسلام فأبى واشتراه العزيز وهو ابن سبع عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same account says Joseph became vizier at thirty, received kingship and wisdom at thirty-three, and died aged 120.
rows.anchor: واستوزره ريان بن الوليد وهو ابن ثلاثين سنة وآتاه الله الملك والحكمة وهو ابن ثلاث وثلاثين سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reports identify Moses’ Pharaoh with Joseph’s Pharaoh, or say Moses’ Pharaoh descended from Joseph’s Pharaoh, citing 40:34.
rows.anchor: فرعون موسى من أولاد فرعون يوسف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts differ on the purchase price: twenty dinars, or a market price equal in weight to musk, silver, and silk.
rows.anchor: العزيز بعشرين دينارا ، وفيل أدخلوه السوق يعرضونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife is named either Zulaykha or Ra’il in reports.
rows.anchor: اسم تلك المرأة زليخا ، وقيل راعيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says none of these biographical reports is established by the Qur’an or a sound report, and exegesis does not depend on them; a careful reader should avoid repeating them.
rows.anchor: لم يدل عليه القرآن ، ولم يثبت أيضا في خبر صحيح وتفسير كتاب الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Honor his residence” means make Joseph’s dwelling and stay pleasant; the noun refers to remaining in a place.
rows.anchor: أي منزله ومقامه عندك من قولك ثويت بالمكان إذا أقمت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The master’s wording honors Joseph’s residence rather than his person, signaling that he regarded him with esteem and reverence.
rows.anchor: أمر العزيز امرأته بإكرام مثواه دون إكرام نفسه ، يدل على أنه كان ينظر إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The master hoped Joseph would help manage their affairs or be adopted as a son; he had no child.
rows.anchor: أي يقوم بإصلاح مهماتنا ، أو نتخذه ولدا ، لأنه كان لا يولد له ولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As God saved Joseph from the well, He enabled him by turning the master’s heart toward him, eventually giving Joseph authority in Egypt.
rows.anchor: أي كما أنعمنا عليه بالسلامة من الجب مكناه بأن عطفنا عليه قلب العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True perfections are power and knowledge: empowerment in Egypt signifies the former, while learning interpretation of reports signifies the latter.
rows.anchor: الكمالات الحقيقية ليست إلا القدرة والعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi allows preliminary divine inspiration (irhas): the revelation in the well could comfort Joseph, ease his grief, and let him enjoy Gabriel’s presence rather than commission him.
rows.anchor: بل لأجل تقوية قلبه وإزالة الحزن عن صدره ولأجل أن يستأنس بحضور جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Joseph’s first revelation may have begun his prophethood, with the later verse describing further revelation and spiritual degrees.
rows.anchor: إن ذلك الوحي الأول كان لأجل الرسالة والنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi interprets “to teach him interpretation” as sending Joseph to convey obligations and call people to true religion, while allowing a reading of progressively increased revelation.
rows.anchor: والمراد منه إرساله إلى الخلق بتبليغ التكاليف

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud names three especially perceptive judgments: the master’s hope for Joseph, Moses’ sister’s advice to hire him, and Abu Bakr’s appointment of Umar.
rows.anchor: العزيز حين تفرس في يوسف فقال لامرأته أكرمي مثواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God prevails over His affair” may mean that none can resist God’s own decree or judgment.
rows.anchor: غالب على أمر نفسه لأنه فعال لما يريد لا دافع لقضائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it means God directs Joseph’s affairs: the brothers intended harm, but God willed good, and His plan prevailed; people often fail to see that all rests with God.
rows.anchor: انتظام أموره كان إلهيا ، وما كان بسعيه وإخوته أرادوا به كل سوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage’s sequence presents Joseph’s empowerment and then his wisdom and knowledge as recompense for patiently enduring the trials caused by his brothers.
rows.anchor: جميع ما فاز به من النعم كان كالجزاء على صبره على تلك المحن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some argue that prophethood is earned through good works, patient effort under trial, and gratitude, since Joseph’s trials are followed by his receiving prophethood.
rows.anchor: النبوة جزاء على الأعمال الحسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects acquired prophethood: the verse does not mean everyone who performs Joseph’s good works receives such offices, since scholars agree prophethood cannot be earned.
rows.anchor: وهذا بعيد لاتفاق العلماء على أن النبوة غير مكتسبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Joseph was never a prophet but merely an obedient servant is false by consensus.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول باطل بالإجماع

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Joseph was a prophet from the revelation in the well, but became a messenger only when granted judgment and knowledge as an adult.
rows.anchor: إنه كان نبيا من الوقت الذي قال الله تعالى في حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Joseph became a messenger from the moment he was cast into the hidden depth of the well.
rows.anchor: إنه كان رسولا من الوقت الذي ألقى في غيابة الجب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says reaching one’s ashudd means attaining the limit of youth and strength before decline; the expression is used for singular and plural.
rows.anchor: تقول العرب بلغ فلان أشده إذا انتهى منتهاه في شبابه وقوته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, places Joseph’s reaching maturity at thirty-three; Razi says this fits medical principles.
rows.anchor: روى ابن جرير عن مجاهد عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human growth resembles the moon: the body grows gradually to full maturity and then declines until nothing remains.
rows.anchor: فإنه يظهر هلالا ضعيفا ثم لا يزال يزداد إلى أن يصير بدرا تاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi maps the moon’s roughly twenty-eight-day cycle into four seven-day stages and analogizes human development to seven-year stages, with maturity around ages twenty-nine to thirty-three or thirty-five.
rows.anchor: مدة دور القمر ثمانية وعشرون يوما وكسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes judgment as practical wisdom restraining desire and knowledge as theoretical wisdom; Joseph’s patient endurance opened practical discipline first, then spiritual disclosures.
rows.anchor: الحكم والحكمة أصلهما حبس النفس عن هواها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the practical-then-theoretical interpretation, childhood bodily fluids initially limit the rational soul; as innate heat matures the body’s instruments, the soul’s practical and theoretical powers and illumination develop.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى استكمال النفس في قوتها العملية والنظرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s exceptional beauty is said to have attracted the woman; another report says her husband was impotent.
rows.anchor: فلما رأته المرأة طمعت فيه ويقال أيضا إن زوجها كان عاجزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rawada” means that either party tried to obtain sexual intercourse from the other.
rows.anchor: إذا حاول كل واحد منها الوطء والجماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: She closed the doors because this deed is done in concealed places, especially when unlawful; commentators say the intensified form reflects seven doors.
rows.anchor: لا يؤتى به إلا في المواضع المستورة لا سيما إذا كان حراما

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi derives aghlaqa from sticking or clinging, and explains it as shutting a door so that opening it becomes difficult.
rows.anchor: في كل شيء تشبث في شيء فلزمه قد غلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators explain the intensive plural “ghallaqat” by saying she shut seven doors.
rows.anchor: غلقت على التكثير لأنها غلقت سبعة أبواب

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi treats hayta as an action word like ruwayda, and all linguists agree it means “come here.”
rows.anchor: هلم في قول جميع أهل اللغة

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows hayta with an open or a kasra-marked ta.
rows.anchor: مفتوحة الهاء والتاء ، ويجوز

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd, as relayed through Ibn al-Tabrizi, says hayta is Hebrew hiyal meaning “come,” which the Qur’an Arabized.
rows.anchor: بالعبرانية هيالح ، أي تعال عربه القرآن

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the word is a Hauranian dialect that reached Mecca.
rows.anchor: إنها لغة لأهل حوران سقطت إلى بكة فتكلموا بها

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari calls this a shared-language parallel, like Arabic words shared with Roman, Persian, Turkish, and Abyssinian speech.
rows.anchor: وهذا وفاق بين لغة قريش وأهل حوران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary: Nafi and Ibn Amir via Ibn Dhakwan have kasra on hāʾ and fatḥa on tāʾ; Ibn Kathir reads it like haythu; Hisham’s cited reading is ahallana; others have open hāʾ, still yāʾ, and open tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن عامر في رواية ابن ذكوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s “ma‘adh Allah” is an absolute seeking of refuge in God; the pronoun in “innahu” is the pronoun of the matter.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله : { أنه } للشأن والحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He calls the master his lord in the sense of master, owner, or benefactor: betraying someone who honored him would be irrational.
rows.anchor: ربي وسيدي ومالكي أحسن مثواي حين قال لك : أكرمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wrongdoers” can mean those who repay kindness with abuse, or adulterers who wrong themselves or put things in the wrong place.
rows.anchor: الذين يجازون الإحسان بالإساءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s use of “my lord” is not a lie: he spoke according to how others regarded him as a slave, and also meant that the master had raised and cared for him, a valid double entendre.
rows.anchor: وهذا من باب المعاريض الحسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi argues the plea for refuge supports his doctrine of divine decree: God’s refuge must create decisive obedience-motivation and remove the motive to sin, beyond capacities and other aids already granted.
rows.anchor: يخلق فيه داعية جازمة في جانب الطاعة وأن يزيل عن قلبه داعية المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi compares the plea to the Prophet’s prayer on seeing Zaynab for God to steady his heart, and to the report that a believer’s heart is between two fingers of the Merciful; the fingers signify motives to act or refrain.
rows.anchor: وكان المراد منه تقوية داعية الطاعة ، وإزالة داعية المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s three-part reply is carefully ordered: God’s rights forbid the act; the benefactor’s kindness should not be repaid with betrayal; and a brief pleasure cannot justify worldly disgrace and severe afterlife punishment.
rows.anchor: حق الله تعالى يمنع عن هذا العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi cites commentators who say Joseph also truly intended the sexual act and sat as a man with a woman before the divine sign removed his desire.
rows.anchor: وجلس منها مجلس الرجل من المرأة ، فلما رأى البرهان من ربه

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: A report through Ali says she desired Joseph and he desired to undo his waist-knot.
rows.anchor: قال جعفر الصادق رضي الله عنه بإسناده عن علي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One Ibn Abbas report says Joseph loosened his belt and sat in a betraying posture; another says she lay down and he sat between her legs to remove his clothes.
rows.anchor: حل الهميان وجلس منها مجلس الخائن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi rejects the culpability reports: al-Wahidi offers no supporting verse or sound hadith, only claims from commentators and extensive unhelpful narration.
rows.anchor: وما ذكر آية يحتج بها ولا حديثا صحيحا يعول عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The correct view, held by verified exegetes and theologians and defended by Razi, is that Joseph was innocent of wrongful action and prohibited intent.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول المحققين من المفسرين والمتكلمين

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi argues that interpreters who affirmed Joseph’s act better understood prophetic rank than those who denied it; Razi criticizes the claim as unsupported.
rows.anchor: والذين أثبتوا هذا العمل ليوسف كانوا أعرف بحقوق الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged conduct combines grave sexual sin, betrayal of trust, repaying extraordinary kindness with disgraceful injury, and harming the benefactor who raised Joseph from childhood; Razi says it is unworthy even of the most corrupt person, much less a prophet.
rows.anchor: مقابلة الإحسان العظيم بالإساءة الموجبة للفضيحة التامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s statement that He turned evil and lewdness away from Joseph rules out the alleged sin, which would be among the worst forms of both.
rows.anchor: أن ماهية السوء والفحشاء مصروفة عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the verse were not decisive, its immense praise of Joseph immediately after narrating a grave sin would be incoherent, like a king praising a servant just after recounting his worst crimes.
rows.anchor: فلا يليق بحكمة الله تعالى أن يحكى عن إنسان إقدامه على معصية عظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets respond to any lapse with remorse and repentance, which God recounts elsewhere; since no repentance is reported here, Joseph committed no sin in this event.
rows.anchor: وحيث لم يوجد شيء من ذلك علمنا أنه ما صدر عنه في هذه الواقعة ذنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every participant confirms Joseph’s innocence: Joseph, the woman, her husband, the witness, God, and even Satan’s exclusion of the sincere from his temptation.
rows.anchor: لهم تعلق بهذه الواقعة يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph claims innocence by saying she pursued him and later asks for prison rather than answering the women’s invitation.
rows.anchor: يوسف عليه السلام ادعى البراءة عن الذنب فهو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman admits to the women that she pursued Joseph and he resisted, and later the women acknowledge that she pursued him.
rows.anchor: ما خطبكن إذ راودتن يوسف عن نفسه قلن حاش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The husband blames the women’s plotting, tells Joseph to leave the matter, and orders his wife to seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: إنه من كيدكن إن كيدكن عظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wording emphasizes Joseph’s purity four ways: the emphatic “to turn away,” explicit “evil and lewdness,” calling him one of Our servants, and calling him sincere or chosen.
rows.anchor: فقد شهد الله تعالى في هذه الآية على طهارته أربع مرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active reading of mukhlasin describes Joseph as sincerely obedient; the passive reading means God selected him for Himself, and both denote freedom from the accusation.
rows.anchor: باسم الفاعل يدل على كونه آتيا بالطاعات والقربات مع صفة الأخلاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan admits he cannot tempt God’s sincere servants; because God calls Joseph one of them, Satan’s own statement supports Joseph’s innocence.
rows.anchor: ويوسف من المخلصين لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الخوارزمي
rows.claim: Al-Khwarizmi’s poem mocks the accusers as former soldiers of Satan who surpassed their teacher in inventing sinful ways.
rows.anchor: طرائق فسق ليس يحسنها بعدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi first argues that Joseph did not intend her at all: “he intended her” is the fronted answer to lawla, meaning he would have done so had he not seen his Lord’s proof.
rows.anchor: لا نسلم أن يوسف عليه السلام هم بها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj objects that placing lawla’s answer before it is non-eloquent and that it should be introduced by a lām.
rows.anchor: شاذ وغير موجود في الكلام الفصيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says a fronted answer is permissible when it is the more important point, citing Sibawayh, and that an answer may appear without lām; he cites 28:10 against al-Zajjaj’s restriction.
rows.anchor: أنه قال : إنهم يقدمون الأهم فالأهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The counterfactual still has a purpose without Joseph’s desire: it shows religious proof, not lack of desire or ability, restrained him.
rows.anchor: ترك الهم بها ما كان لعدم رغبته في النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because lawla calls for a response and the stated phrase can supply it, that phrase should be its answer; an omitted answer is less likely when no single completion is indicated.
rows.anchor: وهذا المذكور يصلح جوابا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even granting that a him occurred, it cannot attach to a person’s essence; an implicit action must be supplied. Razi rejects intercourse and first reads Joseph’s intention as pushing her away and stopping her wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: فاللائق بالمرأة القصد إلى تحصيل اللذة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the push-away reading, the divine proof could warn Joseph that resisting physically would get him killed or damage his garment so the witness might wrongly incriminate him; fleeing preserved the evidence.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى أعلم يوسف عليه السلام أنه لو هم بدفعها لقتلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes him as natural desire, a common idiom for something one wants; desire itself is not the forbidden act.
rows.anchor: وهذا مستعمل في اللغة الشائعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading makes him an inward struggle between natural appetite and reason: like a righteous faster tempted by an iced drink, the pull is not sin, and resisting it displays stronger devotion.
rows.anchor: ورؤية البرهان عبارة عن جواذب العبودية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi faults al-Wahidi for bluster and lists of exegetes without presenting a reasoned proof for attributing the act to Joseph.
rows.anchor: ولم يبق في يد الواحدي إلا مجرد التصلف وتعديد أسماء المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi resists a report that Abraham lied three times: accepting it compromises a prophet’s truthfulness, and rejecting it only risks calling unknown transmitters liars, a lesser concern.
rows.anchor: صون إبراهيم عليه السلام عن الكذب أولى من صون طائفة من المجاهيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He likewise asks al-Wahidi who can guarantee that the narrators attributing the alleged interpretation to earlier exegetes were truthful.
rows.anchor: ومن الذي يضمن لنا أن الذين نقلوا هذا القول عن هؤلاء المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For defenders of prophetic impeccability, the proof may be knowledge of God’s prohibition of adultery and its punishment.
rows.anchor: حجة الله تعالى في تحريم الزنا والعلم بما على الزاني من العقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that God purified prophets’ characters and those close to Him from vile traits, linked to the purification of the People of the House.
rows.anchor: طهر نفوس الأنبياء عليهم السلام عن الأخلاق الذميمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says Joseph saw the prohibition “do not approach adultery” written on the ceiling.
rows.anchor: ولا تقربوا الزنى إنه كان فاحشة وساء سبيلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the proof with prophethood, which would make committing the very vice prophets forbid contradict their mission and invite the rebukes in 61:2–3 and 2:44.
rows.anchor: أن الأنبياء عليهم السلام بعثوا لمنع الخلق عن القبائح والفضائح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who accuse Joseph say the woman covered her jeweled idol out of shame; Joseph replied that he would be ashamed before the living God who sees every soul.
rows.anchor: قامت إلى صنم مكلل بالدر والياقوت في زاوية البيت فسترته بثوب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and several named early authorities say Jacob appeared biting his fingers to warn Joseph against conduct unworthy of a prophet; Razi rejects the story as unsupported.
rows.anchor: نقلوا عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما أنه تمثل له يعقوب فرآه عاضا على أصابعه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: A version from Sa‘id ibn Jubayr says Jacob struck Joseph’s chest, causing his desire to leave through his fingertips.
rows.anchor: تمثل له يعقوب فضرب في صدره فخرجت شهوته من أنامله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account has an unseen voice warn Joseph not to be like a bird whose plumage falls away when it fornicates.
rows.anchor: إنه سمع في الهواء قائلا يقول يا ابن يعقوب لا تكن كالطير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A further Ibn Abbas report says Jacob’s image did not stop Joseph, so Gabriel kicked him and all desire left him.
rows.anchor: أن يوسف عليه السلام لم ينزجر برؤية صورة يعقوب حتى ركضه جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi objects that the reports portray Joseph as ignoring Jacob and Gabriel until physically kicked; he calls such accounts baseless and internally implausible, since even a sinful person would desist from shame at a pious visitor.
rows.anchor: والخذلان في طلب اليقين فهذا هو الكلام المخلص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction makes evil a hand’s assault and lewdness adultery; another makes evil the preliminaries, such as kissing or lustful looking, and lewdness the act itself.
rows.anchor: السوء مقدمات الفاحشة من القبلة والنظر بالشهوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “Our sincere ones” may mean those who sincerely serve God or those whom God has chosen and purified; another possibility links Joseph to Abraham’s purified descendants.
rows.anchor: ومن فتح اللام أراد الذين خلصهم الله من الأسواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir, and Abu Amr read mukhlasin with kasra on the lām throughout the Qur’an; the remaining readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر وأبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two raced to the door: Joseph sought to escape while the woman pursued him to pull him back; each tried to reach it first, as in the phrase “Moses chose his people.”
rows.anchor: ومعناه تبادر إلى الباب يجتهد كل واحد منهما أن يسبق صاحبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph reached the door first; the woman caught only the back of his shirt and tore it lengthwise, whereupon they encountered her husband.
rows.anchor: يوسف عليه السلام سبقها إلى الباب وأراد الخروج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text says “her master,” not “their master,” because Joseph was not truly that man’s slave.
rows.anchor: لأن يوسف عليه السلام ما كان مملوكا لذلك الرجل في الحقيقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her “what is the penalty” may be a negative statement (“his penalty is nothing but prison”) or a rhetorical question (“what could his penalty be but prison?”).
rows.anchor: أي ليس جزاؤه إلا السجن ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her affection makes her mention prison before painful punishment, avoid directly insisting Joseph be punished, and suggest brief confinement; permanent imprisonment would be phrased like Pharaoh’s threat in 26:29.
rows.anchor: لأن المحب لا يسعى في إيلام المحبوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Having seen Joseph resist despite youth and strong desire, she respected his purity and could not explicitly accuse him; Razi contrasts her restraint with later accusers who slander him.
rows.anchor: عظم اعتقادها في طهارته ونزاهته فاستحيت أن تقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Her accusation may allude to Joseph’s attempt to push her away, which would count as harm to her in her framing while she insinuated a sexual assault to others.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك بالنسبة إليها جاريا مجرى السوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph did not expose the woman initially; when she slandered him, he answered to protect his life and reputation.
rows.anchor: ما هتك سترها في أول الأمر إلا أنه لما خاف على النفس وعلى العرض أظهر الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several signs favor Joseph: as their apparent slave he could hardly overpower his master; he was running to escape; she was adorned while he was not; his long conduct showed no such vice; she spoke vaguely while he spoke plainly; and, reportedly, her impotent husband left her desire evident.
rows.anchor: العلامات الكثيرة كانت دالة على أن يوسف عليه السلام هو الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given these accumulated signs, the husband paused and stayed silent because he knew Joseph was truthful and his wife was lying.
rows.anchor: فلما حصلت هذه الأمارات الكثيرة الدالة على أن مبدأ هذه الفتنة كان من المرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s plain assertion and flight, his apparent slave status and long spotless conduct, his lack of adornment, her ambiguity, and the reported impotence of her husband all pointed to her as the instigator.
rows.anchor: العلامات الكثيرة كانت دالة على أن يوسف عليه السلام هو الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the strength of those signs the husband hesitated and fell silent, knowing Joseph truthful and the woman false; the shirt’s tear then supplied further support for Joseph’s innocence.
rows.anchor: استحيا الزوج وتوقف وسكت لعلمه بأن يوسف صادق والمرأة كاذبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same circumstantial signs favor Joseph: his status as a slave, flight toward the exit, lack of adornment, long honorable conduct, direct denial versus her vague accusation, and her husband’s reported impotence.
rows.anchor: العلامات الكثيرة كانت دالة على أن يوسف عليه السلام هو الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the witness was the woman’s wise cousin, who had heard the commotion and proposed judging by whether the shirt was torn in front or behind.
rows.anchor: أنه كان لها ابن عم وكان رجلا حكيما واتفق في ذلك الوقت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view, also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak, makes the witness an infant whom God enabled to speak in the cradle.
rows.anchor: منقول عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما وسعيد بن جبير والضحاك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas counts four infants who spoke: Joseph’s witness, Pharaoh’s hairdresser’s child, Jesus, and the companion of Jareeh the monk.
rows.anchor: تكلم في المهد أربعة صغار شاهد يوسف

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba’i prefers the adult cousin: if God made a child speak, that would itself conclusively prove the woman false, making the shirt test redundant; “from her family” matters only for a probabilistic witness.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى لو أنطق الطفل بهذا الكلام لكان مجرد قوله إنها كاذبة

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba’i also argues that “witness” ordinarily means someone with prior knowledge of the event, supporting an adult who heard the commotion rather than an infant.
rows.anchor: لفظ الشاهد لا يقع في العرف إلا على من تقدمت له معرفة بالواقعة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the witness was the shirt itself, torn at the back; Razi calls this extremely weak because a garment is not ordinarily called a witness or described as family.
rows.anchor: الشاهد كون قميصه مشقوقا من دبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The back tear alone does not prove innocence: a man could have pursued the woman and she might have torn the shirt while chasing him to beat him; it only strengthens the many other signs.
rows.anchor: أنا بينا أن علامات كذب المرأة كانت كثيرة بالغة مبلغ اليقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who saw the shirt may be either the husband called her master or the witness, so the referent is disputed.
rows.anchor: وذلك يحتمل السيد الذي هو زوجها ويحتمل الشاهد فلذلك اختلفوا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling women’s plotting great is no contradiction: women’s scheming in this domain is great relative to humans, and it brings a kind of dishonor that men’s schemes do not.
rows.anchor: كيد النسوات بالنسبة إلى كيد البشر عظيم ولا منافاة بين القولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Joseph, turn away from this” is attributed either to the husband or to the witness; it tells Joseph to conceal the incident and prevent a damaging scandal.
rows.anchor: أعرض عن ذكر هذه الواقعة حتى لا ينتشر خبرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife’s being told to seek forgiveness may mean asking her husband to pardon her, which favors the witness as speaker; alternatively, it means asking God, which allows the husband as speaker.
rows.anchor: ويكون معنى المغفرة العفو والصفح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If forgiveness means seeking God, Joseph’s reference to God as the one, conquering Lord shows that those people affirmed a Creator while worshipping idols.
rows.anchor: إلا أنهم مع ذلك كانوا يعبدون الأوثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling her “one of the erring” suggests habitual wrongdoing and that her husband already knew her tendency to misconduct.
rows.anchor: وهذا أحد ما يدل على أن الزوج عرف في أول الأمر

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأصم
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Asamm says the husband was not very jealous, since he was satisfied with asking her to seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: إن ذلك لزوج كان قليل الغيرة فاكتفى منها بالاستغفار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the masculine plural “erring” as grammatical predominance of males, or as saying her disposition descended from an erring lineage.
rows.anchor: تغليبا للذكور على الإناث
